item.title: Netflix, Fox and the $2bn bid for the 2030 World Cup that could reshape live sports
item.description: The battle for the US TV rights to the tournament will pit the traditional broadcaster and the ‘whatever-it-takes’ streamer. It could be a tipping point in the industry The awarding of broadcast rights in the United States for this year’s World Cup was a cut-price deal to avoid legal action from the existing rights holders, Fox Sports. This week’s tender process for the 2030 tournament will be anything but. Media rights and broadcast experts canvassed by the Guardian in the US and Europe are united in agreement that Fifa will benefit from the most competitive and expensive auction in the competition’s history. It is expected to fetch between $1.5bn (£1.13bn) and $2bn, with some predicting the outcome could be a landmark moment for the sports and entertainment industry. Continue reading...

item.title: ‘When I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West’: the two lives of Bromley footballer Omar Sowunmi
item.description: Full-time defender and part-time model, the 31-year-old is happy to shine a light on both sides of his dual career “I was walking down the street one day and someone came up to me and said: ‘I think you should be a model,’” the Bromley defender Omar Sowunmi says. He was already living out many people’s dreams as a professional footballer but was able to assume an alter ego in the world of fashion. There are few parallels between the grind of lower-league football and Milan fashion week but the 31-year-old is adept in both worlds. Sowunmi’s dual career mixes trips to Doncaster with visits to Paris. On Saturday Bromley travel to Reading under their new manager, Karl Robinson, as they attempt to move off the bottom of League One and the centre-back is clear where his focus lies even after his chance encounter with a model agency employee expanded his horizons. item.title: Jack Grealish recalls a golden age of mavericks – but football has moved on
item.description: Everton forward has magical talent and popularity to burn, but has come up against hard reality of the modern game Thomas Tuchel has never called up the player he once claimed to love “everything about”. The reason for Jack Grealish’s omission from Tuchel’s first England squad in March 2025 was given as “he simply has no rhythm”. Catch a falling star? Grealish was suspended by Everton for three matches following “a breach of club discipline”. Suggestions his loan from Manchester City might be cancelled were calmed by David Moyes. Last week, Grealish played in a behind-closed doors friendly against Derby before issuing an Instagram statement: “I want to apologise to the fans and everyone at the club for not being able to help the team the last few weeks.” Amid tabloid tales of karaoke nights and extended socialising, how close is the former boy wonder, now 31, to blowing it? item.title: Victor Wembanyama’s ridiculous self-assisted dunk steals the show despite Spurs’ 105-93 loss to Pistons
item.description: Photo by Ronald Cortes/Getty Images Victor Wembanyama produced another highlight-reel moment against the Detroit Pistons, throwing the ball off the backboard before catching it and finishing with a one-handed dunk. The San Antonio Spurs star used his incredible height and creativity to get past Ausar Thompson early in their meeting with Detroit. Wembanyama had already been blocked by one of the Thompson twins this season, but he found a different way to attack the basket this time. Victor Wembanyama’s self-assisted dunk steals the show against Detroit Pistons The 22-year-old drove towards the paint just over a minute into the game before sensing pressure from Thompson. Rather than force his way through the defence, Wembanyama threw the ball against the backboard, collected it in the air and threw down a one-handed finish. It was a reminder of the unusual skills that make the Frenchman such a difficult player to defend. At 7-foot-4, Wembanyama has the size to dominate near the rim, but his ability to improvise makes him even more dangerous. He entered the contest averaging 28.6 points and 11.6 rebounds through 14 appearances, ranking third and fifth in the NBA in those categories respectively. However, the highlight did not tell the full story of the night for San Antonio. Despite Wembanyama finishing with 25 points and 18 rebounds, the Spurs fell to a 105-93 defeat against Detroit at the Frost Bank Center. Dylan Harper added 20 points, while Julian Champagnie scored 14. Detroit also had the final say in the battle of the big moments, with Cade Cunningham producing a poster dunk over Wembanyama near the end of the first quarter. The defeat leaves San Antonio with a 12-3 record after starting the season strongly. Tonight, that defensive touch was massive in containing the Raptors’ shooting and regularly contesting their attempts. Bridges was active on this end throughout the game, making that quiet impact even when he wasn’t scoring. item.title: Greenwich holds off Ridgefield for 4th straight Class LL girls swimming title, 33rd overall
item.description: Greenwich is ready to dive into the pool at the Cornerstone Aquatics Center in West Hartford after capturing the Class LL girls swimming championship on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. (Kevin Roberts/Hearst Connecticut Media) WEST HARTFORD - The Greenwich and Ridgefield girls swimming and diving programs have engaged in plenty of battles over the years, and the CIAC Class LL championship meet on Tuesday night at the Cornerstone Aquatics Center was no different. For the Cardinals, depth turned out to be key as they captured their fourth straight Class LL title and 33rd overall in program history. Greenwich scored 924 points to second-place Ridgefield's 878.5. Amity was third with 510.5 points. "I felt pretty confident going into this because I knew that everyone on the team has been working super hard, and I had a lot of faith in us," Greenwich junior Olivia DeVries said. With sophomore Alden Charette's first-place finish in Class LL diving, the Cardinals won three individual events and one relay. Seniors Kensie Worden (50 freestyle, 23.59) and Julia Kozma (100 butterfly, 57.70) won gold medals, as did the opening 200 medley relay team of Charette, junior Sara Jee, Kozma and Worden (1:47.96). Greenwich claimed 18 individual medals, including three golds, three silvers and three bronzes. DeVries claimed bronze medals in the 200 freestyle and 500 freestyle. "I'm super proud of the team because we all have worked so hard in practice. The captains have done such a good job to keep us motivated and I'm just very proud of how hard we worked," DeVries said. "Every single swimmer made a difference, every single spot. If you were in the C final, the A final, everyone makes a difference. We are all cheering for each other, and I think that's what makes Greenwich special." "We had some really great swims from all the girls, but especially our senior class," Greenwich coach Megan Kelly said. "I think it really means a lot to them, and to see them swim with such heart was really great." Senior Ellison Charette was second in the 200 IM and 500 freestyle, and she was part of the second-place 200 and 400 freestyle relay teams. "Ellison, she fought hard in both of her races. She had some really good swims. Overall, I was really, really pleased," Kelly said. "They didn't win the (200) free relay, but they went 1:35, which is All-American consideration time. That was pretty impressive." Greenwich's second-place 200 freestyle relay finished in 1:35.79. Ridgefield's first-place relay of sophomore Zsofia Milak, senior Dalia Katra, sophomore Mary Kelly and junior Ellie Griffin swam the race in 1:35.21, which broke Ridgefield's 2022 state record of 1:35.48. Milak had a terrific night for Ridgefield, winning individual gold medals in the 200 freestyle (1:50.20) and 100 freestyle (50.95). She was also part of the first-place 400 freestyle relay (3:32.60), along with Kelly, junior Chloe Archibald and sophomore Charlie Palmer. Kelly won the 500 freestyle in 4:59.44. Norwalk/McMahon

item.title: Gilbert Arenas claims ‘heartless’ Klay Thompson’s Megan Thee Stallion breakup led to resurgence
item.description: Photo by Raymond Hall/GC Images Klay Thompson is finding himself delivering at a level many fans got accustomed to during his prime with the Golden State Warriors. Earlier this year, Thompson ended his relationship with rapper Megan Thee Stallion, which became quite a pop culture controversy. And given how well Thompson is playing since joining the Miami Heat, Gilbert Arenas believes the breakup has helped him find his form again. Gilbert Arenas believes Klay Thompson is returning to form thanks to Megan Thee Stallion breakup Speaking on The Arena show, Gilbert Arenas spoke about Klay Thompson’s recent return to form from a shooting standpoint. Arenas suggests that the nature and fallout of his recent breakup with rapper Megan Thee Stallion has somehow given him the confidence he needs to once again become the elite shooter he once was. “One of the greatest shooters of all time not having his shot, when that’s what you do for a living… Sometimes, certain type of minds need certain things,” Arenas said. “I think the Megan Thee Stallion (situation), just watching someone like, ‘this is the worst break-up I’ve ever had,’ made him sleep good at night. The old Klay is back!” “Sometimes, in the movie, that killer has a soft spot, and he’s more vulnerable… He just lost his touch. When he’d seen that, and she was all distraught, he probably sat back like, ‘Yeah. This is me. When they’re crying at the doorstep, my shot is back!’ “I just really believe that’s all it took. Looking at the phone, talking about, ‘I hate your guts,’ and he’s thinking, ‘Yeah, I’m about to have 30 tonight!’ Everything is back. “Klay is back! The killer is back! Keep shooting the ball, baby, and keep breaking hearts! You’ve got to add that part to it. He shoots like he’s heartless! Gotta keep breaking hearts!” This season, Thompson is averaging 15.5 points, 2.1 assists, and 1.4 rebounds, while shooting 45.1% from the field and 43.4% from beyond the arc. Thompson has hit 50+ three-pointers in just 13 games this season, the fastest he has reached this mark at any point in his NBA career. item.title: Cade Cunningham makes a bold claim after leading the Pistons in snapping the Spurs' streak
item.description: Cade Cunningham makes a bold claim after leading the Pistons in snapping the Spurs' streak originally appeared on The Sporting News . Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here . Heading into Tuesday's game between the Detroit Pistons and the San Antonio Spurs , the latter were the overwhelming favorites. The Pistons faced a tough game, especially without Duncan Robinson. However, the Pistons shocked the world by taking control and winning. They snapped the Spurs ' 12-game winning streak, and Cade Cunningham was at the center of it all. Cade Cunningham cements the Pistons as a top team once again As one of the best point guards in the NBA, Cunningham has proven to be a fantastic player for the Pistons. He has been their leader for a while now, and he is delivering on his potential from being drafted first overall in 2021. Since then, the Pistons have gone through all kinds of struggles, but also some solid successes. They were the first seed in the Eastern Conference in the 2025-26 season, but their early exit from the Playoffs has led to doubts. With this performance against the Spurs, the doubters were silenced. MORE: Cade Cunningham is calling out the people who doubted him and the Pistons Cunningham has affirmed that the Pistons are ready for the team to hit another level. They are ready to prove that they are still one of the best teams in the league, and they are ready to go toe-to-toe with the top teams like the Spurs. "It was a group effort; everybody had to bring it. I like my guys; we do this together every day. We love basketball; we all come from grit, to get to this point... Nobody in that locker room has fear in their heart for anybody," Cunningham said on the NBC broadcast after the big win . Winning against a team like the Spurs is a big achievement, and Cunningham was key to that. However, he is the first one to credit his team for helping him beat the Spurs, one of the toughest tasks any team has ths season. item.title: Knicks coach Mike Brown compliments Raptors coach despite him mocking Jalen Brunson during clash
item.description: Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images Toronto Raptors head coach Darko Rajakovic made it clear that he was not a fan of New York Knicks guard Jalen Brunson flopping during their game. The Knicks picked up a 111-102 win over the Kawhi Leonard-less Toronto Raptors on November 17 to improve their record to 8-6 for the season. Brunson is overcoming his slow start to the season and put up 31 points, five rebounds and five assists in the win. However, his on-court antics seem to run Raptors coach Rajakovic the wrong way. Mike Brown impressed by Darko Rajakovic even after he mocked Jalen Brunson’s flopping during Knicks vs. Raptors Rajakovic was caught on camera imitating Brunson for flopping after a shot, with cameras catching how openly Rajakovic mocked Brunson after that play. Nonetheless, Brown was positive about Rajakovic after the game . “Darko does a heckuva job…those guys play hard, really good defensively, give us fits. I thought our execution, especially down stretch at a pretty high level both ends of the floor, in particular, offensively… Our pace, spacing, screening, take care of basketball down stretch. Brunson had the last laugh, leading the Knicks to a much-needed win over the Raptors and establishing themselves as an East contender after a slow start to the season. Brunson is averaging 27.0 points, 5.9 assists and 2.9 rebounds this season, and shooting 7.2 free throws per game. He ranks 11th in free-throw attempts this season, so his flopping hasn’t helped him get to the line much. Brunson’s scoring is the key offensive weapon the Knicks are built around, evidenced by his performances in their run to the 2026 NBA Championship. While Rajakovic did not do anything excessive in terms of complaining about Brunson’s actions, he did display his feelings in a hilarious fashion. This was Toronto’s fifth straight loss of this season, falling to 5-9 on the season. Rajakovic has the support of the organisation and likely felt comfortable calling out Brunson with his gesture instead of biting his tongue. However, complaining about calls will not change the Raptors’ fortunes this season, as evidenced by the loss to the Knicks. item.title: Awkward Jim Harbaugh-Justin Herbert Moment Adds Weird Vibe To Chargers Win
item.description: Justin Herbert trade rumros Getty It took nine games, but the Los Angeles Chargers got their first win of the 2026 regular season on Monday night against the Baltimore Ravens. A 1-8 record is not much to celebrate, and an awkward moment in the locker room after the game between head coach Jim Harbaugh and quarterback Justin Herbert just gave the whole thing a very weird vibe. In a video shared on social media which can be viewed here, Harbaugh congratulated the team for the win and then implored everyone to give each other a high five. The camera catches Harbaugh and Herbert exchanging a high five where the signal caller did not look all that enthused as he lightly exchanged a high five with his head coach. Some on social media saw the moment as evidence that Herbert doesn’t like Harbaugh or that he doesn’t have a good attitude. Others defended Herbert, asking whether he should have been doing back flips for their first win of the season. It’s probably just a moment that got blown way out of proportion but when a team has had as terrible a season as the Chargers, every single little moment is going to be scrutinized whether it is fair or not. To give Herbert the benefit of the doubt, it has been a brutal season. He probably doesn’t want to be celebrating too hard when his team is just having a completely embarrassing year. Plus, Herbert has always been fairly mild-mannered and reserved. Mina Kimes wrote a whole profile about Herbert years ago for ESPN which delved into how he is an introvert and just simply isn’t the big personality that many people expect an NFL quarterback to be. Herbert and Harbaugh really do not mix on paper That is what makes the Herbert-Harbaugh pairing so interesting on paper. Harbaugh is loud, bombastic, and prone to outbursts. Herbert is serene, cool, and supremely understated. It wouldn’t seem like the two would work together well but sometimes opposites attract in relationships. The last two seasons the two seemed to work together quite well as the team went 11-6 and made the playoffs each season. Maybe the addition of offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel is what threw things off a bit but Herbert has remained steadfast in his support of his offensive playcaller . Maybe the moment in the locker room is evidence of Herbert showing his displeasure with his head coach, or maybe it’s just how Herbert is. He and Harbaugh are completely different personality-wise so most likely it is just a case of two very different people sharing a bit of an awkward moment which wouldn’t even be blinked at if the team was 8-1 rather than 1-8. item.title: Duke hits new low in 37 years with blowout loss to Illinois
item.description: Mandatory Credit: Rob Kinnan-Imagn Images Duke hits new low in 37 years with blowout loss to Illinois appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . History has the receipts proving Duke is a basketball powerhouse . However, nobody is completely invincible. On Tuesday, No. 5 Duke reluctantly welcomed No. 10 Illinois to the famed Cameron Indoor Stadium in Durham, North Carolina. The Illini defeated the Blue Devils 99-78. It was not only a blowout loss, but also the first of its kind in a long time for Duke, per Joe Tipton of On3Sports.com. The last time the Blue Devils lost by more than 20 points at home was in 1989, 37 years ago, to be exact. Additionally, the Blue Devils ‘ 35-game winning streak at home came to an end. Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) Duke had not lost at home by 20 points since 1989, a span of 37 years. The Blue Devils’ 35-game home winning streak, the longest in the nation, is also over. Historic win for Illinois. This group is connected, tough, and fearless. Brad Underwood has a dangerous group. https://t.co/WkERFMjFN1 — Joe Tipton (@JoeTipton) November 18, 2026 Illinois came ready to play. A major factor was Andrej Stojakovic scoring a record 46 points , the most points scored by an opponent at Cameron Indoor Stadium since Grady Wallace scored 43 points for South Carolina in 1957. Despite their size and height, Duke was outrebounded by Illinois in a 54-34 win. The Illini also grabbed 18 offensive rebounds and scored 19 second-chance points. Plus, Illinois won the battle in the paint, 48-30. They also put up 22 points off 14 Blue Devils turnovers. The Blue Devils shot 24-for-64 from the field (37.5%) and 9-for-40 from 3 (22.5%). They were also only 21-for-33 from the field and missed 12 free throws. For Duke, freshman center Joaquim Boumtje-Boumtje led the way with 17 points and five rebounds. Senior guard Caleb Foster added 15 points and six rebounds. Second-year guard/forward Sebastian Wilkins added 10 points. The Blue Devils are now 3-2. They enter the season trying to shake off an Elite Eight exit to UConn after being the No. 1 seed. On Saturday, the Blue Devils will play against Utah in Pittsburgh. A former WNBA player, she currently serves as Boston’s vice president of team operations and organizational growth. She joined the Celtics in 2019 after an accomplished professional playing career. Her work has focused on player development, organizational culture and relationships throughout the basketball operation. Jabour offers a different background. The Kings executive has worked extensively in scouting, player evaluation and roster construction. Before joining Sacramento, he held a scouting leadership position with the Philadelphia 76ers. Riccardi, meanwhile, previously served as an assistant general manager with the Mavericks. He also spent more than a decade with the Brooklyn Nets organization, including a stint running their G League affiliate. Following Nico Harrison’s dismissal in Dallas in November 2025, Riccardi and Michael Finley briefly shared interim general manager responsibilities. All three candidates bring NBA experience, although Indiana has not announced a finalist or identified a preferred choice. Fever Planning One Hire After Major Leadership Shake-Up The Fever’s search began after team president Kelly Krauskopf stepped down Oct. 23. General manager and chief operating officer Amber Cox departed later that day, leaving Indiana with significant vacancies in basketball leadership. However, Philippou clarified that the Fever intend to hire one basketball executive rather than separate replacements for Krauskopf and Cox. That distinction is significant. The incoming executive will inherit a franchise with championship expectations and several consequential personnel decisions approaching. Krauskopf helped build the Fever from their inception and guided the franchise through its first WNBA championship in 2012. Cox, meanwhile, oversaw basketball operations during a period of heightened attention surrounding the team’s young core. The timing of Indiana’s search adds urgency to the decision. Caitlin Clark remains the centerpiece of the franchise, while Kelsey Mitchell enters another important offseason following a career-best 2026 campaign. Mitchell’s upcoming free agency presents an immediate challenge for whoever takes charge. The four-time All-Star has established herself as one of the WNBA’s premier scorers, making her future a central question in Indiana’s plans. The next executive must also evaluate the roster around Clark and Mitchell while working with coach Stephanie White to establish a sustainable championship contender. Indiana’s leadership changes have created uncertainty. Tuesday’s report, however, suggests the search is entering its final stages. With several NBA-connected candidates under consideration and a decision expected within weeks, the Fever could soon have the person responsible for guiding their next chapter. item.description: Dale Earnhardt Jr. fires back at Chase Elliott crew chief criticism. item.description: Nov 17, 2026; Durham, North Carolina, USA; Duke Blue Devils guard Caleb Foster (1) reacts on the bench during the second half against the Illinois Fighting Illini at Cameron Indoor Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Rob Kinnan-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect First of all, there’s no doubt that Illinos deserved the win at Cameron on Tuesday night. The Illini just thumped the Blue Devils in almost every way. They outrebounded Duke, 54-34, and Duke had 14 turnovers. Illinois also outscored Duke 31-21 from the line, and ruthlessly controlled the paint. Duke took 40 threes in this game, hitting just 9. Illinois shot just 6-32, but their control of the paint made that irrelevant. And so did the performance of Andrej Stojakovic. When Duke played Cal in 2024, Stojakovic finished with 10 points on 4-14. Tuesday night, he lit Duke up for 46 points on 14-21/2-3 from the floor, along with 16-20 from the free throw line. It was a record-breaking performance: the most points ever scored by an opponent in Cameron was 43 by South Carolina’s Grady Wallace in 1957, when the ACC was 3 years, 9 months, and 15 days old. It came perilously close to breaking Dick Groats’ record of 48 points, set in 1952. He was superb and nearly unguardable, but he’s not the only reason that Illinois won. Quentin Coleman racked up 27, but it was more than that. Here’s something you may not have caught: Zavier Zens, cousin of Kon and Kager Knueppel, who is 6-7, got 8 rebounds. He out-rebounded every Duke player who got on the floor. So did Coleman, who is 6-4, and so did reserve Stevan Vaaks, who, like Zens, is 6-7. JoJo Boumtje Boumtje got 5 rebounds. He’s 7-2. Patrick Ngongba got 4 rebounds. He’s 6-11. Cameron Williams, 7-0, got 3. Drew Scharnowski, 6-10, got 2. You could argue that Duke’s second five outplayed the starters. Cameron Williams came in and almost immediately blocked two shots. The reason he did it was because he was angry at his coach, Mike Krzyzewski, who had challenged him in some pretty elemental ways, as we understand it, and Jones wanted to make a point. We’re not sure how Scheyer will do that, but it might need to be done. And in fairness to Boumtje Boumtje, and we’re not picking on him, but the kid is 17. He’s adapting to a very new situation. Let’s give them both time and space to figure that out. The reality though is that in sports, there’s a goal, and that goal is to win. As we saw in the second half, sometimes changes need to be made. He added: “For almost a decade, the fallout from these events, or from those events, has remained part of the conversation around Australian cricket. It has been a difficult chapter for many people, and increasingly, the ongoing debate has become a distraction for our game. We believe it is time for a circuit breaker.” Boon repeated that the forum is not intended to revisit the past in a legal sense, and he closed with a call for unity. “This forum is not about re-litigating the past at all. It’s about creating an opportunity for those who wish to be heard to tell their stories in a respectful, safe environment, and for our sport to listen.” “Australian cricket is at its strongest when we’re united, and we owe it to everyone who loves the game to make every reasonable effort to move forward together with understanding, respect, and perspective.” Cricket Australia Interim Chair David Boon announced the establishment of a forum for players to discuss their sandpapergate experience. PRESSER ➡️ https://t.co/3LYlghFwsz https://t.co/aHaKPGuoKL — Telegraph Sport (@telegraph_sport) November 18, 2026 Is Cricket Australia re-opening the Sandpapergate investigation? Greenberg’s answer The short answer from the board is no. Greenberg confirmed that the original 2018 investigation will neither be reopened nor made public, with confidentiality given as the reason. Greenberg said the game is hurting right now, and then spoke about the need to recover. “It’s not good for anyone. We need to find a path through, and we need some time to heal.” He also made clear what the new process is and is not meant to do, and he repeated that taking part is a personal choice. He said: “As part of this process, and so that all parties who wish to can tell their version of events, we have set up now an independent forum. He wants the public to hear the full story, and he believes that is impossible unless every person involved speaks. He said: “I have always wanted a safe space to chat… I also have some questions about Cricket Australia because the public wants to know what happened there. It’s hard to get the whole truth unless everyone is speaking.” MORE: Akram questions Australian bowlers' 'didn't know' defence in Sandpapergate He then said he does not want to see anyone punished, and he raised a concern about what the board will do with the material. He further asked: “I don’t think there should be any sanctions… the board makes the decisions but what comes out at the end? I have a really good relationship with Todd Greenberg, and I respect what he’s trying to do there. "But at the end of the day if you’re going to cherry-pick what is said in this report, the board can choose whatever they want to come in, or come out. Are we just going in a circle here? That’s the thing I’m not sure about.” Warner, who was speaking alongside Khawaja, also ruled out any desire for further penalties. He pointed to what the players accepted at the time and to what he sees as the real purpose of the forum. He said: “We put our hands up, we accepted what Cricket Australia handed out to us. It’s not about penalties. It’s about transparency and accountability - which Todd’s acknowledged, on CA’s behalf, about the culture at the time with the players and CA.” MORE: 'Tried eradicating it': Cummins admits Australia of 2018 had a 'win at all costs' mentality A forum without a published outcome may not settle the Sandpapergate debate The board’s intention is easy to understand, because nearly a decade of argument has simply worn people down. A confidential, voluntary forum offers a way for everyone to speak without the threat of sanctions, and that is a reasonable starting point. However, the same features that make the forum safe may also limit its value. Khawaja has already pointed out the central weakness: CA will decide what is released at the end. If the public sees only a short summary, those who want answers are likely to treat it as a polished version of events, and the debate will carry on. The voluntary nature of the process is a second problem. Cummins and Starc have strongly rejected Khawaja’s version, and if they choose not to take part, the forum will hear one side of the dispute far more than the other. A discussion with missing voices is unlikely to produce the shared understanding Boon hopes for. CA can improve its chances by publishing the terms of reference early, by naming a respected independent figure, and by being clear about what will be shared. item.title: Cincinnati schedules home-and-home with Missouri for 2027 and 2032
item.description: HOUSTON, TX - NOVEMBER 07: Cincinnati Bearcats football helmet rests on the visitors' sideline during the college football game between the Cincinnati Bearcats and Houston Cougars on November 7, 2026 at TDECU Stadium in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Leslie Plaza Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images While the 2026 regular season is in its twilight stages, some teams are already looking ahead to 2027. On Tuesday, Cincinnati and Missouri announced a home-and-home non-conference series. Missouri will host the Bearcats at Faurot Field on Sept. 18, 2027, while Cincinnati welcomes the Tigers to Nippert Stadium on Sept. 11, 2032. Although the campuses are separated by fewer than 500 miles, the 2027 matchup will mark the first-ever meeting between the Big 12 and SEC opponents. Cincinnati has now finalized its non-conference schedule for the 2027 season. The Bearcats will host Central Connecticut of the FCS on Aug. 28, remain at home against Missouri State on Sept. 4, and complete their non-conference slate at Missouri on Sept. 18. Cincinnati does not have a game scheduled for the weekend of Sept. 11, when it will either play its Big 12 opener or take a bye. Both Missouri and Cincinnati experienced recent cancelations in their 2027 non-conference slates, making them a perfect match for each other. The Tigers saw their 2027 home contest against Illinois get axed, while Cincinnati’s looming road trip to Boston College was also removed from the schedule. The Bearcats have won five consecutive regular season non-conference matchups, sweeping all three opponents during the 2026 season. The 2027 trip to Missouri will mark the program’s first true road non-conference game since Sept. 14, 2024 when it traveled to crosstown rival Miami (OH). Also, it will be the Bearcats’ first out-of-state non-conference road game since Sept. 9, 2023 at Pittsburgh and first SEC matchup since Sept. 3, 2022 at Arkansas. Cincinnati traditionally had one non-conference vacancy reserved for Miami, as the two competed in one of the longest running series in college football. The rivals played their 129th and final scheduled meeting this past September, making it the fourth-most played FBS matchup behind Minnesota-Wisconsin, Auburn-Georgia, and North Carolina-Virginia. Although an iconic rivalry has been shelved, the Bearcats can look forward to securing their first victory over SEC competition on Sept. 18, 2027 in Columbia.

After just two years in charge of the USMNT (and a whirlwind two years at that), Pochettino departs to take up the coveted / cursed position of Manchester United manager. It’s a change that’s as disappointing as it is unsurprising. Despite the misty-eyed soundbites over the last week in which he described the decision as “one of the toughest” of his career, Pochettino’s return to club football has felt inevitable. He made no bones about his wandering eye, always quick to profess his love for the Premier League while maintaining his London residence throughout his time with the USMNT. Even when his contract extension was announced this summer, the conditions of that deal made it abundantly clear that should an attractive suitor come calling, he would answer. Now, after years apart, he'll get to rekindle that romance. As Pochettino celebrated Christian Pulisic putting the U.S. ahead in the 25th minute with one of the most acrobatic goals of the attacker's career (a high-flying bicycle kick that cut the ball inside the far post), some of his personnel were already across the Atlantic, laying the groundwork for his upcoming rendezvous. Even if his couching staff was divided, Pochettino insisted that his focus was not. And with Julian Hall doubling the USMNT's lead in the 43rd minute, perhaps he wasn't lying. It’s rare that football managers exit on their own terms. Even rarer still when they finish out their tenure having already secured their next job. Likely rarest of all, is to go straight from a CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final to the biggest derby in English football. Then again, little about Pochettino's tenure has been normal. To even appoint the Argentine, U.S. Soccer aimed higher, spent more, and was bolder than ever before. The mechanisms employed to secure his signature (including donations-as-salary from hedge-fund billionaire Ken Griffin) were as opportunistic as they were canny. Ultimately, they succeeded. But has Pochettino? If this window is anything to go by then the answer is emphatically yes . Eight goals, zero conceded, across two competitive performances is beyond reproach. Exciting attacks, the promise of youth, undeniable tenacity - much of what fans hoped they would get from Pochettino's appointment was on display against Haiti. But stepping out of the moment, things become a little more complicated. Pochettino’s time as U.S. head coach saw no records broken and no trophies won. The USMNT's ranking is identical to when he took over while his win percentage is less than that of predecessor Gregg Berhalter. Meanwhile, his relationship with the players (Christian Pulisic, in particular) was at times tense, and his rapport with media and fans could even be patronizing. It was, however, also under his watch that 78 different players earned a cap, nine teenagers made debuts, and the USMNT put in one of their all-time great performances (Paraguay), World Cup or otherwise. Altogether, it's a portfolio that plays like a Rorschach test. Love him or hate him, you'll find stats to back you up. But stats aren't really where Pochettino's legacy lies. Indeed, what Pochettino left the U.S. with - and perhaps even the wider soccer world - was a shift in perception. The US can should think bigger. Our talent is plentiful. World Cups are winnable. How true these notions actually are remains to be seen, but what isn’t up for debate is who promoted them: Mauricio Pochettino. USMNT head coach Muaricio Pochettino. The sheer reality of that fact makes any future fantasies just a little more plausible. It's something that even Pochettino seemed to recognize. “Being head coach in USA now is prestigious,” he said. Self-aggrandizing, sure, but also true - even if only symbolically. And this, more than anything, is Pochettino’s great success. Two years ago, the thought of a top-tier, globally in-demand manager taking over the United States men's national team was unthinkable. International football simply wasn't a jewel in the managerial crown - let alone a program as disparaged as the U.S. But one Pochettino later, and the narrative has changed. Now, some of the biggest names in soccer (Tuchel, Carlo, Klopp) find themselves helming national teams (England, Brazil, Germany, respectively) while arguably the biggest name is rumored to be intrigued by the prospect of taking over the USMNT. The likelihood of Pep Guardiola becoming the next United States head coach is slim, at best. But what's remarkable is that it's no longer laughable. This is a massive country, with tremendous resources, and enormous potential. The scale and scope of a USMNT "project”, combined with the prospect of unleashing a sleeping giant, might actually entice a name as big as Pep (see Man City). Still, in the immediate context of Haiti and a Nation's League quarter final, it's a prospect that's hard to reconcile, and, ultimately, a reflection of the unique place that the U.S. now finds itself. A place where B.J. Callaghan is mentioned alongside Julian Nagelsmann. Where the self-deprecating backwaters of USMNT fandom have turned a little less dark. Where the once overlooked now get second glances. A place that was good enough for Mauricio Pochettino.

item.title: Pocognoli’s aspiration for how Scotland must play is in danger of becoming unworkable
item.description: The 4-0 debacle against Switzerland has added to the tactical concerns about the head coach’s suitability, just six games into the job The Scottish Football Association can only cling to a lesson from the past when assessing a worrying international window. Steve Clarke was beleaguered during his early games in charge. Successive 4-0 defeats by Belgium and Russia in 2019 left Clarke with the sense he should have stayed in club management. A revival meant Clarke led his country to three out of four tournaments. There are, however, fundamental differences between the story of Clarke and that being delivered by Sébastien Pocognoli. Clarke was a pragmatist, whose decades in coaching suggested he had the wherewithal to revive Scotland. Pocognoli, six games into his tenure, is in danger of lurching into the territory of dreamy ideologue whose aspiration for how Scotland must play is unworkable. The meek nature of Scotland’s collapse in the 4-0 loss to a second-string Switzerland was lamentable. The Belgian’s assessment, with overpraise a key theme, raised eyebrows. Continue reading...

item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Barely six weeks ago, Jürgen Klopp’s big home debut in the Germany dugout ended in a deeply frustrating 1-0 Nations League defeat to Greece – but the manager tasked with returning Die Mannschaft to relevance claimed not to care. “I’m completely unbothered,” Klopp trilled unconvincingly. “I’ve lost far more matches than I would have liked, but as long as you draw the right conclusions, a loss is ultimately a piece of information – no different from a win.” It was a quote straight out of the Pierre Sage playbook for unfussed continental coaches – and probably worried a few German FA suits, given Klopp had already threatened to quit at his own unveiling over potential media intrusion and criticism. “If you say tomorrow, ‘he’s [sh!t]’, tell me to my face and I’m out,” Klopp roared to trembling hacks in July . That imagined confrontation now looks unlikely to take place, because his Germany side are suddenly very good indeed. Continue reading...

item.description: A new film about the historic World Cup quarter-final clash finds new angles for a new generation “Is there anything new to say about it?” Gary Lineker asked the producer Flora Fernandez-Marengo when she first approached him to take part in The Match, a documentary about the 1986 World Cup quarter-final between England and Argentina. The rock’n’roll angle, with Brian May as a talking head, is one of the very few details the film-makers added to Andrés Burgo’s book, The Match, on which the documentary is based. The directors Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco play with the timeline, hopping between past and present across 91 minutes, the exact duration of the match itself. Anecdotes that now form part of Argentina’s football folklore are spliced with excellent archive material. Continue reading...

item.title: Do good club managers necessarily make good international managers? | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: In a mailbag edition of our newsletter, we look at Mauricio Pochettino, Pep Guardiola’s international credentials and the lack of elite English managers Sign up for our free newsletter here Who should replace Mauricio Pochettino as the USMNT manager? – Tom S Although the salary I’m sure will be excellent, I think the US job is going to be a really difficult sell to a top-level coach. The 2030 World Cup is a long way away and I’m not sure the Concacaf Nations League, the Gold Cup or even the 2028 Copa América carry much appeal for a manager with European experience or aspirations. But I’m not entirely sure that sort of coach is necessarily a great idea. The last two World Cups, after all, have been won by low-key coaches who have come from within the federation and have worked with many of the players at youth level. That’s the positive from appointing from within; appointing from without is almost certainly more expensive and there’s the danger the next foreign manager does just what Mauricio Pochettino does, and has his head turned by the first vaguely attractive European job that comes calling. item.title: Familiarity of Doha drives home just how far Socceroos have come in recent years | Joey Lynch
item.description: There is increasing evidence of an evolution not only in approach but also mentality, highlighted by a return to the scene of Asian Cup heartbreak Last week’s 3-0 dismissal of Qatar at the Abdullah bin Khalifa Stadium marked the first time the Socceroos had returned to the Gulf state since their heartbreaking elimination from the Asian Cup just under three years ago. Back then, coach Graham Arnold called Doha a “home away from home” after they relocated there during the Covid pandemic, and went so far as to suggest that they would have some form of advantage at the 2022 World Cup as a result. Wandering around the city in 2026, memories rush back of Socceroos fans becoming eager participants in the takeover of the city’s souks during the World Cup. So too the feelings of sadness to see the birds still cooped up in small cages at the nearby bird market. It evokes recollections of trips on the red Metro line out to the Al Janoub Stadium in Al Wakrah, aided by the faded posters and stickers celebrating the 2022 tournament’s arrival that to this day can still be seen in shopfronts. There’s the excitement, for some, when a stray cat reminds you just how personable the local felines can be, as well as the sense of unease that remains whenever one pauses to reflect on how all this was built and the hands that did so. item.description: Blues beat champions after bold substitution and Gunners’ home struggles continue with fifth consecutive WSL draw Sonia Bompastor attempted to deflect suggestions that the removal of Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes into Chelsea’s top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City was tactical, but few were convinced by the claim that it was down to injury. The manager said the centre-back, who had not asked to come off and walked straight down the tunnel, had taken a knock to the head in training and been assessed and cleared, but that during the game “she was not herself”. On came Veerle Buurman and the threat of Khadija Shaw was nullified, the Dutch defender restricting the golden boot favourite so well that Shaw did not manage a shot on target. Bompastor said after the game that she had not spoken to Buchanan but that she would “explain myself to her”. “I always have good relationships with the players, bring them clarity, and I’m always direct and honest so they have the information,” she said. “It won’t be any different.” Enforced or not, the substitution was a huge gamble that paid off, even after the loss of Melvine Malard to injury in the first half reduced their number of remaining in-game substitution windows to one. item.title: Three Lions’ win over Spain comes in two acts: the first superb, the second heroic | Sid Lowe
item.description: Visitors take game to world champions and, though their hold on possession plummets, their rearguard is outstanding In the final, absurdly tense moments before England finally did it and Spain finally fell, when Dan Burn had been sent on to do Dan Burn things, when the board had gone up with a 4 on but the clock wasn’t moving fast enough and the men in red kept coming back, Harry Kane had come to the side of the pitch to stand beside Thomas Tuchel. Palms out, Kane signalled and directed and appealed with his teammates to hold on to what they had: s omehow, anyhow . What they had was special, but their grip on it was not as secure as it had seemed. Not as secure as it should have been too. Tuchel gave Kane a nudge that looked pretty playful considering the pressure, before Marc Bollengier, the fourth official, ordered him back to the bench. But England’s captain was not gone for long and when he returned he was joined by almost all of them, awaiting the big moment. From there, he watched James Trafford make an astonishing double save, a moment of heroism that allowed them to hang on. Then, standing alongside the rest who could no longer just sit there, he saw the last header clear – Dan Burn things – before the whistle went. Then he and they went on one last run, back on to the pitch. Continue reading...

item.title: AFC Wimbledon, a failed £87m investment bid and the challenge for fan ownership
item.description: Clubs with wealthy proprietors can maintain a loss-making operation but things can be more complex when the supporters carry the can When you walk up from Haydons Road railway station to Plough Lane there is a blue AFC Wimbledon billboard that reads “Fan owned football”, directly opposite the site of the old Plough Lane stadium where there are now blocks of flats. There is a memorial to the old Wimbledon FC – a reminder that supporters can often have little say in the running of their club – on the same corner, just up the road from the new Cherry Red Records Stadium. AFC Wimbledon are one of only two majority fan-owned clubs in the EFL – along with Exeter – but that makes running a loss‑making operation, as 94% of teams in England’s top five tiers are doing according to the State of the Game report, even more challenging. “In other clubs, the owner just puts their hand in their pocket, produces cash,” said Hannah Kitcher, who has been a member of the Dons Trust Board, which runs AFC Wimbledon, for seven years. “It’s harder when the owners are fans – you can only go to them so many times.” Continue reading...

item.title: Football comes together across Spain to honour Jesús de Miguel: ‘We’ve seen how fragile life is’
item.description: Across La Liga and beyond this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them In the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt. “This is very important,” Ante Budimir began as the dressing room, their sanctuary, fell silent around him. “We don’t have this shirt today for the sake of it. He was not chosen, and nor are we. It could have happened to anyone, anyone. Let us go knowing that we’re grateful to be on the pitch: playing, watching, warming up, sitting on the bench, whatever it may be. Boys, we were not chosen: not us, not him. Let us go, gratefully. Without thought. We have a grand day before us.” With that, Osasuna’s players turned left out of the room, where they were joined in the tunnel by footballers from Athletic Club, rivals from the north, and together they went out past the little shrine of Saint Fermin on to the field. They carried white lilies and all wore the same white shirts with a No 9 on the back, a black ribbon and the name of Jesús de Miguel, the Tenerife striker who died after a collision on the pitch five days earlier at the age of 30. At almost exactly the same time, 2,000km away to the west, Tenerife’s squad were walking out at the Heliodoro Rodríguez López in Santa Cruz. They did not have anyone alongside them, wore black suits not white shirts and did not have a game to play either, not this week. Continue reading...

item.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
item.description: Delap’s talents resurface in style, Gómez delights Brighton with more fireworks, and hair-pulling confusion at Everton It would have been very easy for Oliver Glasner to lose patience with Liam Delap. The forward is still only 23, yet the days when he was rattling in 12 in a Premier League season for Ipswich have come to seem a very long time ago (and his six games for Manchester City even longer). A season at Chelsea had left him bereft of confidence, an odd mix of diffidence and overaggression, devoid of composure in the box, arms flailing like a broken windmill. But the old gifts have not left him. Both goals on Saturday were the result of great muscular surges and if the first finish seemed essentially about hitting the ball as hard as possible on target, the second was a precise – and still powerful – finish in off the far post. After games such as this it’s possible to imagine him as England’s long-term replacement for Harry Kane. item.title: Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row
item.description: The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year. Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running , but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.
